1	1
Grammar Summary Part 3
Bac
Parallelism
 Parallelism refers to making sentences have the same or parallel structures.
 Repeating the same form, tense, or structure is what we call parallelism.
 Traveling is fun, amusing, and a recreational activity.
➔ Traveling is fun, amusing, and recreational.
 We should limit our emissions of greenhouse gases and using renewable energy sources.
➔ We should limit our emissions of greenhouse gases and use renewable energy sources.
 Online learning allows you to study anytime and wherever you are.
➔ Online learning allows you to study anytime and anywhere.

-- 1 of 14 --

© TakiAcademy.com
2	2
Grammar Summary Part 3
Bac
Conditionals
Zero Conditional
When the sun goes down, it gets dark.
→The simple present is used in both clauses.
→ It is used to talk about things that are always true.
1st Conditional
If it’s a nice day tomorrow, we’ll go hiking.
→If+ simple past and will + infinitive.
→ It is used to talk about possible situations.
2nd Conditional
If I were rich, I would buy a big house with a pool.
→If+ simple past and would + infinitive.
→ It is used to talk about ‘unreal’ or impossible things.
→ The situation is unlikely to happen.
3rd Conditional
If I’d studied harder at school, I would have gone to university.
→If + past perfect and would + present perfect
→ It describes something that did not happen.
→ It usually expresses regret.

The Passive Voice
Rule: To be in the right tense + past participle of the main verb
The passive is used when:
The doer of the action is unknown.
➔ The bank was robbed.
➔ The handbag was made in Japan.
➔ Flying cars will be created.
The focus is on the action itself rather than the doer.
➔ My car has been repaired.
➔ The milk was bought from a huge farm.
➔ Insulin was discovered by Frederick Grant Banting.
To talk about general truths.
➔ Rules are made to be broken.
➔ The best olive oil is made in Tunisia.
➔ Sooner or later, the truth will be revealed.
Construction
Tense Active Passive
Simple present Many people follow this
influencer.
This influencer is followed
by many people.
Present progressive Right now, they are baking
chocolate cookies.
Right now, chocolate cookies
are being baked.

The Inversion
What?
Inversion just means putting the verb before the subject.
When?
 To Ask Questions
Steve is a lawyer.
➔ Is Steve a lawyer?
They have been to Australia.
➔ Have they been to Australia?
 With Negative Adverbials
 Put emphasis.
 Has a surprising or striking effect.
 Sounds quite formal.
➔ Rarely have they been abroad.
If you do not want to give this impression (sound formal), you can put the negative expression later in the
sentence in the normal way. → They have rarely been abroad.
 With Inverted Conditional Forms
More formal.
If you had told me about the issue a few days before, I would have been able to help you.
➔ Had you told me about the issue a few days ago, I would have been able to help you.

Reporting questions
 Yes/ No questions
“Did you travel to Egypt last week?”
➔ She wanted to know if I had traveled to Egypt the week before.
➔ She wanted to know whether I had traveled to Egypt the week before.

The Subjunctive
Uses
 To express urgency or importance.
 Give a piece of advice.
 It is very formal.
❖ In spoken English, the subjunctive mood may not be referred to as it is very formal. Thus, you may
hear native speakers adding an “s” to the verbs in the third person.
Examples
I recommend (that) she arrive on time.
➔ The verb “arrive” is in the bare infinitive.
It is recommendable (that) she be on time.
➔ The verb “be” is in the bare infinitive.
The negative form
The doctor suggested that he not smoke.
➔ The word “not” comes before the verb “smoke”.
Verbs Followed by the Subjunctive
Recommend/ demand/ advise/ ask/ request/ desire/ propose/ commend/ order/ insist/ urge, etc.
Expressions Followed by the Subjunctive
To be desirable (that)/ To be recommendable (that)/ To be essential (that)/ To be imperative (that)/ To be
crucial (that)/ To be important (that)/ To be necessary (that)/ To be vital (that)/ To be critical (that)/ To be
of the utmost importance (that)/ To be urgent (that), etc.
Examples
➢ I insist that she leave the corporation!
➢ The doctor advised that Jake buy organic food.
➢ It is crucial that he tell the truth.

Restrictive Vs. Nonrestrictive Clauses
A relative clause is usually introduced by the relative pronouns that, who, whom, which, or whose.
A relative clause modifies a noun or a noun phrase.
A relative clause connects ideas by using pronouns that relate to something previously mentioned.
A relative clause allows the writer to combine two independent clauses into one sentence.
There are two types of relative clauses: restrictive and nonrestrictive.
Restrictive clause Nonrestrictive clause
❖ A restrictive clause modifies the noun that
precedes it in an essential way.
❖ It provides key, identifying information
about the noun it describes.
→ It cannot be removed from a sentence
without changing the sentence’s meaning.
 The man who saved Lily’s life is
Pakistani.
 The world is a book, and those who do
not travel read only a page.
❖ Restrictive clauses are essential, so no
commas are added.
 Would you share the recipe that your
grandma taught you?
That vs. which
For restrictive clauses it is better and clearer to
use “that” and not “which”.
 The arrow that has left the bow never
returns.
❖ A nonrestrictive clause describes a noun in a
nonessential way.
❖ It provides additional but optional
descriptions that can be excised from a
sentence without altering its meaning or
structure.
 Christopher, who has three kids, is a
published writer.
❖ Nonrestrictive clauses are removable, and
commas mark the removable part of the
sentence.
 Brain Drain, which is the flight of human
capital, is a double-edged weapon.
That vs. which
For nonrestrictive clauses it is better and clearer
to use “which” and not “that”.
 TakiAcademy, which provides online
courses, is very popular among the
student population.

Punctuation Marks
Period (.) Question mark (?) Exclamation point (!)
 Called a full stop in British
English.
 As sentence ender.
➔ People need to use public
transportation to reduce the
emissions of carbon dioxide.
 After an abbreviation.
➔ Dr. Jeffrey Lang was born on
Jan. 30, 1954.
 N.B. In British English, no
period is added after
abbreviations, such as Dr,
Mr, Mrs, etc.
 Indicate a direct question.
➔ When will people stop
polluting the environment?
 Called an exclamation mark
in British English.
 To express a sudden outcry.
Within dialogue.
➔ "Oh my God!" screamed
Janice.
 To emphasize a point.
➔ Henry always manages to get
on my nerves!
Comma (,) Semicolon (;) Colon (:)
 Direct address.
➔ You are the best, Jennifer.
 Separation of two complete
sentences.
➔ Cars are getting more and
more expensive, and people
are becoming more and more
dependent on them.
 Separating lists or elements
within sentences.
➔ Jeffrey Lang wrote several
books, including Struggling
 To connect independent
clauses. It shows a closer
relationship between the
clauses than a period would
show.
➔ Jane decided to leave her
corporate job; she was
feeling exploited and
drained.
 After a word introducing a
quotation, an explanation, an
example, or a series.
➔ I need you to email me three
documents: your CV, your
transcripts, and your
diploma.
 Between independent
clauses when the second
explains the first, similar to a
semicolon.

 Two types: en dashes and em dashes.
✓ En dashes: about the width of an upper-case
N.
 Used with a compound modifier that
includes a multi-word element that cannot
easily be hyphenated.
➔ Pre–Industrial Revolution techniques.
 To show ranges of numbers, such as times,
page numbers, or scores (I will schedule
you from 2:30–3:00). But, outside of
formal printed publications, this type of en
dash is commonly replaced with a simple
hyphen.
✓ Em dashes: about the width of an upper-case
M.
 Can be used in place of a comma,
parenthesis, or colon to enhance readability
or emphasize the conclusion of a sentence.
 To join two or more words together into a
compound term (not separated by spaces).
➔ Full-time, well-known, face-to-face, one-on-
one.
 Remember, a compound modifier only needs a
hyphen when it comes before a noun. If it
comes after the noun, leave the hyphen out.
 Do not use a hyphen when you have a
compound modifier that consists of an adverb
ending in -ly plus a participle or adjective.
 When you have a compound modifier that is
interrupted by some other word that’s not
really part of the modifier, use a suspended
hyphen. (Check the section of compound
adjectives for examples).
 Used in numbers.
➔ Thirty-three/ seventy-two/ fifty-four.

 Hyphens are also commonly used to divide

continue on the next line. Book and newspaper

Zero Conditional
When the sun goes down, it gets dark.

→ It is used to talk about things that are always true.
1st Conditional
If it’s a nice day tomorrow, we’ll go hiking.
→If+ simple past and will + infinitive.
→ It is used to talk about possible situations.
2nd Conditional
If I were rich, I would buy a big house with a pool.
→If+ simple past and would + infinitive.
→ It is used to talk about ‘unreal’ or impossible things.
→ The situation is unlikely to happen.
3rd Conditional
If I’d studied harder at school, I would have gone to university.
→If + past perfect and would + present perfect
